requirement: The bundled skills MUST direct agents to make a requirement distributed only when its obligation applies on its own at each of many sites, such as a convention every validation function follows; to use `{impl}` instead when particular code carries out the requirement as a whole; and to mark with `{impl}` the code that carries out any obligation of a distributed requirement that its sites do not uphold.
rationale:
structural: `requirements.cli.distributed_guidance.when` has no structural obligation. Its one obligation is that the bundled skills "MUST direct agents" to do three things:

- Make a requirement distributed only when its obligation applies on its own at each of many sites.
- Use `{impl}` instead when particular code carries out the requirement as a whole.
- Mark with `{impl}` the code that carries out any obligation its sites do not uphold.

Each of these is about what the guidance says. The text names no library, algorithm, signature, type, field, or delegation through a named interface.

I tested each clause against a rewrite that keeps the guidance but changes how it is built. Splitting the guidance across other bundled skill files, rewording it, or reorganizing the sections would all still direct agents the same way. So where the guidance sits and how it is written is a discretionary choice. The text constrains only what the skills tell agents.

The supplied root is `assets/skills/habeas/references/distributed-requirements.md`. I read its outline: a `Distributed requirements` section with Queries, Do, Don't, Gotchas and Review subsections. That is documentation content. Whether it conveys the three directions is behavioral and belongs to the behavioral criterion. It is not something an `{impl}` marker has to establish. No implementation evidence is required here.

behavioral: The requirement has three directions for the bundled skills. Each one is checked by `tests/authoring_cli.rs#fn[bundled_skills_make_a_requirement_distributed_only_for_per_site_obligations]`, which carries a `{test}` reference to the subject.

The test reads the `## Do` section of the habeas skill's `references/distributed-requirements.md`. It does this through the helpers `distributed_reference`, `section` and `assert_text`. `assert_text` asserts that the collapsed section text contains each required phrase, so a missing phrase fails the test. I did not need the implementation source.

1. **Distribute only for per-site obligations.** The test asserts the phrase "Make a requirement distributed only when its obligation applies on its own at each site".
2. **Use `{impl}` when particular code carries out the requirement as a whole.** The test asserts the phrase "when particular code carries out the requirement as a whole, use `{impl}` there".
3. **Mark with `{impl}` the code that carries out obligations the sites do not uphold.** The test asserts the phrase "Separate obligations each site upholds from obligations particular code carries out, and mark that code `{impl}`".

The skill text is static content, so asserting the exact guidance phrases in the section that carries it is an adequate check. The example of a convention every validation function follows is illustrative only and binds no behavior. The text does not distinguish any other input classes or boundaries. I found no behavioral obligation left without a test.
